newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak bourse to launch derivatives trading in Nov.
newsitem.headline: Slovak bourse to launch derivatives trading in Nov.

text.p: The Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) said it would launch derivatives trading in November, but traders and analysts were ambivalent over the project's prospects for success in the fledgling Slovak market.

"The Bourse chamber expects to start trading derivative instruments on the BSE in mid-November, beginning with futures on exchange rates between the Slovak crown and U.S. dollar and German mark," Ondrej Ivanco, head of the BSE trading division said in an interview for Wednesday's edition of the Hospodarske Noviny economic daily.

Money market traders and analysts welcomed the move, saying it would help develop the market and inject competition, but stock brokers said share trade remained too illiquid for derivatives to take off.
Ivanco said the BSE wanted to trade derivatives on all three Slovak capital markets - money, foreign exchange and stocks.
"Other products which should be available soon after the launch of trading are options and futures on the main index, the SAX," he said.
The BSE then plans to expand its actvities to options on selected liquid shares, but Ivanco said the bourse was not planning to trade derivatives on bonds.

"It is a very positive step, regarding all three markets, and it will bring competition for the banking sector which has already been providing some derivative instruments," said Branislav Matusek of Slovenska Sporitelna.

Matusek, however, said he expected trade in derivatives on money market instruments and exchange rates to be more lively in the early days than trade in stock derivatives, arguing that the share market still lacked the necessary liquidity.
Vladimir Kuklis of CSOB Bank said trading derivatives was a condition for further development of the organised capital market, adding the move would help increase transparency.
"Apart from the fact that the settlement of agreed deals will become safer, I see the main advantage of derivatives in covering brokers' open positions," Kuklis said.
However, Dusan Sykora, stock broker at ING Barings, saw little future for stock derivatives on the BSE.
"For example, it is absolutely impossible to fix derivatives on the SAX, as its structure and the market itself allow easy manipulation of share prices and thus also of the index," he said.
Becuase of the low liquidity, brokers can move share prices in very low volume trading.

"And we can forget about futures or options on shares, as even those stocks that we call blue chips, such as steel maker VSZ, oil refiner Slovnaft or fund VUB Kupon, are not liquid enough to quote derivatives on them," Sykora said.
Furthermore, he added, there was still no law in Slovakia that would allow dealing with foreign currencies on the BSE.
"It may work (derivatives on exchange rates), but they have to sort out this legislation problem, and they do not have so much time left until November," Sykora said.
